note: PROPOSED, NOT RATIFIED. A record of convergent independent arrival, written at the moment it was observed rather than after. Seven claims across six repositories state the same rule about privilege — a capability is granted one at a time, opt-in, never implied by a broader grant, and unknown names are refused rather than ignored. None cites another. This is a construction warrant in everything but its storage: the recipe, the digest, and the check procedure are all here, and decision_warrants is still empty for the reason given in the last decision below. §3.2 of the operator's plan says this must be recorded BEFORE the memory infrastructure is pointed inward, because a lookup is inheritance and later agreement carries no evidential weight. A machine may propose this; only a human may confirm it.

warrant.recipe: sha256 over the newline-joined, lexically sorted row_sha256 of the seven claims below
warrant.check_procedure: Resolve each origin (repo@sha:path#anchor). Read the seven docstrings. Verify (a) each states the rule in its own vocabulary for its own lane, and (b) none cites, imports, or references another — that independence is the whole claim. A citation found between any two reduces the count by one and the warrant must be recomputed.

claims.states: mcp:<server_id>:<tool> — permitted() stays a literal name lookup, 'which is what makes the ACL auditable'; a grant for one federated tool never implies another
the own-line rule as a property rather than named instances: no capability flag may be a member of any permission group

consent granted one flag at a time, per packet kind; 'consent is opt-in, so this is the only way a contact ever gains a permission — nothing on the wire may grant one'; unknown flag names rejected rather than ignored
what the adapter saw but the Event must not carry, held by the Guard and 'released only capability-by-capability, with a logged justification'
I-12 — a context window's rung is the max of everything in it, including neighbours a semantic search pulled in; the non-escalation half of the same rule, so retrieval cannot launder a lower rung
rows that declare servable=True and cannot be proven so — declaration-versus-enforcement as a computed column over a whole set; the conformance-evidence face of the rule
the principled REFUSAL of per-kind: 'deliberately not a per-kind allow-list — that would be a second copy of cascade.LEDGER_KINDS to keep in step, and a kind missing from it would under-count'

decisions.question: What did seven lanes independently arrive at?
decisions.commitment: That a privilege must be granted one at a time and never implied — and that the enumeration must not be a second copy of an authority that already exists. Six of the seven state the positive rule in their own vocabulary for their own lane: MCP tool grants, manifest capability flags, LAN packet kinds, quarantined event fields, context-window rungs, and servable-row declarations. The seventh states the constraint on the rule, and states it by refusing an application of it.
decisions.why: The lanes have no shared abstraction and could not have inherited this from one another: u2u gates signed LAN packets between nodes, corpus-lens gates fields the Guard holds back from an Event, homestead gates what a prompt's rung may be raised to by retrieval, terpsi-music gates which records may be served, willow-mcp gates what a manifest may unlock. They are separated by org boundary, by transport, and by threat model — u2u's adversary is a second person in the room, willow-mcp's is an agent authorising itself. Arriving at the same shape from those starting points is what makes the shape load-bearing rather than stylistic, which is the argument evidence.py:56 already makes about PROVENANCE_STATES and decision 53ee54c2 calls 'what independent necessity produced'.

decisions.question: Why is the counter-instance evidence FOR the rule rather than against it?
decisions.commitment: Because it refuses per-kind enumeration for the same reason the others adopt it: a hand-maintained list drifts from the authority it copies. Nestor declined a per-kind allow-list because it would be a second copy of cascade.LEDGER_KINDS and a missing kind would under-count. The rule is not 'enumerate per kind'; it is 'the enumeration must be the authority, never a copy of one'. Under that reading all seven agree, and the two decisions differ only in where the authority already lives.
decisions.why: Measured the same day, in willow-mcp: KNOWN_PERMISSIONS restated three of gate.py's six capability flags by hand, and the three it omitted — task_db, mcp_federation, grove_relay — were enforced by permitted() and grantable by nobody. The federated lane was unreachable from the day it was written. That is nestor's predicted failure, realised in the repo that also holds the positive form of the rule. The fix (PR #396) was to derive the set from gate rather than restate it a third time — the same move nestor made, reached independently and after paying for it.

decisions.question: What does the pairing of the two willow-mcp claims show that neither shows alone?
decisions.commitment: That the own-line rule has two halves and only one was enforced. test_authority_surface.py asserted no capability flag is INSIDE a permission group — the safety half, which prevents over-granting. Nothing asserted that every capability flag is GRANTABLE — the usability half. mcp_federation satisfied the first and failed the second for weeks, and the suite stayed green throughout. Both halves are now derived from the same gate constants, in two tests kept apart because they fail for different reasons.
decisions.why: A rule enforced in the direction of safety and unenforced in the direction of usability produces controls nobody can operate, which look identical to controls that work. That is the same defect as the nine forgery tests in Jeles skipped behind one module-level importorskip, and as ratify() documenting itself operator-only while exposing no operator command. A control that has never been exercised is an assertion, not a control.

decisions.question: Why is this recorded as a decision document rather than attached with nestor warrant attach?
decisions.commitment: Because warrant.attach requires a pair_id and this finding is not a translation pair — it is a claim about seven corpus rows across six repositories. The warrant's substance is complete and stored above (kind, authority, expected_digest, recipe, check_procedure, and the seven locators), so a reader can perform the check today; only its row in decision_warrants is missing. That table remains at 0 rows.
decisions.why: The gap is worth naming rather than working around: the warrant machinery can vouch for an answer but not for a structural claim about the corpus itself, and structural claims are exactly what a survey produces. Either warrants grow a subject other than a pair, or findings of this shape need their own home and this document is it. Recorded now regardless, because §3.2 is a one-way door — once the memory infrastructure is pointed inward, a seventh lane agreeing is inheritance rather than arrival, and the evidence cannot be reconstructed after the fact.
